title: Without honor at home (Mark 6:1–6)
hook: his hometown asks, isn't this the carpenter? and he can do little there

segments.voice: Yesterday, two Aramaic words: talitha koum, little girl, get up. Your line was care goes on to the kitchen.

You go home for the holidays. You've changed, learned things, maybe become someone new. And within an hour at the table, you're twelve again. Somebody brings up the time you broke the window. Jesus has healed crowds, calmed a storm, raised a child. Then he walks back into Nazareth, the village he grew up in, and teaches in the synagogue on the sabbath. And the people who watched him grow up can't get past who he used to be.
screen: `HOME FOR THE HOLIDAYS.` → `BACK TO NAZARETH.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO KNEW HIM.`

segments.voice: At first they're amazed. Where did he get all this? Then, in the old King James Bible, the questions turn: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" They name his brothers, James, Joses, Judas and Simon, and say his sisters are right here with us. "And they were offended at him." Mark is the only gospel that calls Jesus himself the carpenter; Matthew says the carpenter's son. The Greek word is tekton, a builder who works with wood and maybe stone: doors, roofs, plows, yokes. Jesus worked with his hands, probably for most of his adult life, in a village of a few hundred people where everyone knew the builder. How can the man who might have fixed our door be a prophet? Jesus answers with a line that became a proverb: "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house." Then one of the most striking sentences in Mark: "he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk, and healed them." Could. Not would. Matthew, telling the same story, says he did not do many. And "he marvelled because of their unbelief." Usually the crowds marvel at him. Here he marvels at them. Early copyists seem to have found it uncomfortable too: some manuscripts of Mark change the question to the son of the carpenter. Many Christians read the scene as a sign of how much trust matters, and how familiarity can close a door. And many find it comforting that the Son of God had a hometown that didn't get him, and a trade, and calluses.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` · `TEKTON — A BUILDER WITH HIS HANDS.` · `A PROPHET, AT HOME.` · `HE COULD DO NO MIGHTY WORK THERE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've known so long you've stopped really seeing them: a sibling, a parent, an old friend, a spouse. Notice the old label you carry for them, then ask what might be true about them now that you've missed, something they've learned, or carried, or become. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Tekton, the Greek word for builder: the trade of the man his hometown couldn't see past.
Your line: isn't this the carpenter? The people closest can be the slowest to see. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Christians honor Jesus's years as a working craftsman, and Catholics keep a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1; churches often draw on this story when talking about faith at home and at work.

chat.meaning: Nazareth knew him as the tekton, the village builder, and couldn't see past it. Familiarity closed a door.

notes: Audit (10% sample): stated-as-fact claim that neighbors had hired Jesus softened to 'might have'; filler 'Christians have long pondered this' replaced with the manuscript detail that some copies of Mark 6:3 read 'son of the carpenter' (P45 and others, assimilating to Matthew); confirm.
KJV 6:3 reads 'Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James...'; the quotation ends at 'Mary' with a question mark added for speech. Confirm acceptable.
Brothers named again (James, Joses, Juda, Simon); churches' differing views were given on day 170 and are not repeated. Confirm that's enough.
τέκτων: builder/craftsman, 'wood and maybe stone'; confirm.
Matthew 13:58 'he did not many mighty works there' vs. Mark 6:5 'could there do no mighty work'; confirm.
